query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Co‐free, as‐solidified FeNiCrMn alloys, nanoscale Mn‐based oxide precipitates (formed during rapid solidification) act as structural mediators by impeding dislocation motion and delaying dynamic recrystallization. This precipitate‐controlled mechanism is responsible for preserving a favorable strength–ductility balance across a wide range of temperatures and strain rates.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐solidified FeNiCrMn with a fine, homogeneous grain structure and a uniform distribution of nanoscale Mn‐based oxide precipitates, along with a high dislocation density from rapid solidification.
generation.intervention: Apply dynamic mechanical loading (e.g., tension and/or compression) tests at systematically varied temperatures (from room temperature up to ~900 °C) and over a range of strain rates.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under controlled atmospheres using samples prepared under rapid solidification conditions to ensure similar precipitate distribution and dislocation densities. A comparison will be made with samples that are heat-treated to dissolve or coarsen the Mn‐based precipitates.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale Mn‐based oxide precipitates acting via Orowan strengthening and Zener drag.
generation.mechanism: At low to moderate temperatures (25–600 °C), the fine precipitates contribute to strengthening by obstructing dislocation glide and favoring slip/twinning mechanisms, while at higher temperatures (≥700 °C), they impede grain boundary migration and delay dynamic recrystallization (via Zener drag), thereby sustaining dislocation forest hardening and overall strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The as‐solidified alloy with retained nanoscale precipitates will exhibit high yield strength with a balanced ductility over the temperature range and a delayed onset of dynamic recrystallization compared to heat‐treated samples lacking these precipitates. This behavior should manifest as a measurable shift in the dynamic stress–strain response and microstructural evolution under high-temperature, high-strain-rate conditions.
generation.baseline: Dynamic mechanical behavior of the as‐solidified FeNiCrMn alloy with full precipitate retention (control group) compared to similar alloy compositions subjected to post-solidification heat treatment that dissolves the precipitates.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to FeNiCrMn alloys processed under similar rapid solidification conditions where the precipitate formation is inherent; it may not extend to alloys with significantly different defect states or impurity levels resulting from alternative processing routes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of the precipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution on delaying recrystallization and strengthening, especially under varied strain rates, remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrMn alloy samples with identical base compositions: one set as‐solidified (retaining nanoscale Mn‐oxide precipitates) and a second set subjected to a heat-treatment designed to dissolve or coarsen the precipitates. Subject both sets to controlled dynamic loading tests (compression/tension) across a temperature range from 25 °C to 900 °C and at multiple strain rates. Use complementary microstructural analyses (TEM, EBSD) alongside mechanical testing (stress–strain curves, yield strength, ductility measurements).
measurements: Grain size and recrystallized fraction (via EBSD)
Precipitate size and volume fraction (via TEM/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples (with reduced or coarsened precipitates) display the same dynamic mechanical response—specifically, a similar strength–ductility balance and similar onset temperature for dynamic recrystallization—as the as-solidified samples with abundant nanoscale precipitates, then the hypothesis that Mn-based oxide precipitates are the primary mechanism controlling the dynamic behavior is falsified.

Question: What are the temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation mechanisms of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) compared to conventionally processed alloys?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using pre-alloyed spherical powder (average diameter 27.2 µm); laser power 90 W, scan speed 600 mm/s, hatch space 80 µm, layer thickness 25 µm, volumetric energy density 75 J/mm³, 180° rotation scanning pattern, high-purity Ar atmosphere.. Test conditions: Compression tests at 25, 500, 600, 700, 800, and 900 °C; initial strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹; engineering strain limit 0.4; specimens preheated at 10 °C/min; MoS₂ lubricant used..
